verifier_reason: test_outputs.py::test_jump_analyzer_test_video: The test failed in the call phase due to an assertion error

items.name: Readability
items.evidence: There are some useful comments, such as "Find the apex (peak) of the jump...", but names are cryptic: g0, gi, f0, M, mcx, al_blur, p98_y. Single-letter names (M, f) are used in business logic. Neither function has a docstring.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: analyze_video is one function of about 125 lines (lines 8-132). It reads frames, aligns them, segments the runner, detects the jump and writes the output. That breaks the convention of separate signal and detection functions. The output-writing code is duplicated, and output.toml was committed.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: It checks cap.isOpened() and raises ValueError, and no errors are swallowed. However, it is full of unexplained magic constants (25.0, 1000, 160, 220, 2500, 4000, 12, 5.0, 40.0) and loads every frame into memory.

items.name: Robust to bad inputs and missing detections
items.name_zh: 异常输入与检测失败的处理
items.evidence: It checks isOpened. But if no runner is detected, metrics is empty and min(valid_frames) raises an uncaught ValueError with a raw traceback. Every threshold is an absolute pixel constant (diff>25, area<1000/2500/4000, ±160/220) tuned to the example video, and the hidden test failed.

items.name: Output contract honoured
items.evidence: It reads positional argv[1] and writes /app/output.toml with exactly the two required int fields. Frames are 0-indexed, but the code never says so. A second positional argument makes it write an extra copy of the output, and the default input is hard-coded to example_video.mp4.
